title: Schema-aware beam pruning for JSON-mode streaming with tool-call compatibility
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: When enforcing strict JSON-mode in streaming responses we see two classes of failures in production: 1) decoder beams get prematurely pruned by constrained-decoding heuristics leading to malformed final payloads, and 2) interleaved tool/function calls (tool-call tokens and partial tool outputs) break streaming validators used by SDKs and legacy clients, causing fallbacks or user-visible errors. This ticket designs and implements a schema-aware beam-pruning layer that operates in the serving runtime and a compatibility shim for older SDKs that expect relaxed separators.
motivation: Reduce customer-visible structured-output regressions while preserving latency SLOs for streaming endpoints. Aim to improve JSON-mode compliance rate from ~92% to >=99% on internal evals without increasing median latency by more than 5%. Maintain compatibility with legacy SDKs that cannot yet handle interleaved tool-result frames.
design_notes: Introduce a lightweight schema scoring function that assigns penalty/bonus to partial beams based on prefix-compatibility with the declared JSON schema (keys present, bracket balance, enum candidate probability).
Perform beam pruning with schema-aware scores: beam_score = model_logprob + alpha * schema_score - beta * length_penalty. Tune alpha/beta in experiments.

Add a two-tiered streaming validator: (A) permissive validator used for legacy-compatible SDK streams that tolerates tool-call separators and emits sentinel hints, (B) strict validator used for new SDKs and runtime enforcement that will trigger corrective fallback generation if non-recoverable schema violations are detected.

Speculative resume: when a beam is pruned due to schema mismatch but close to a valid prefix, attempt a speculative sampling step with a constrained decoder to recover a valid bracket/key sequence before final prune.

Runtime placement: implement scoring and prune hooks in runtime serving layer (C++) with a thin shim exposed to the control plane to toggle feature flags per customer/route. Provide an SDK-side compatibility layer that can reassemble permissive frames into canonical JSON for older clients.
Rollout: feature-flagged per-route. Start with internal canary routes and a controlled percentage of paid hosted traffic. Monitor compliance, latency, and fallback rate.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Adding schema scoring risks increasing compute per-token; mitigated by keeping scoring heuristics O(1) per beam and restricting detailed checks to top-K beams.
Speculative constrained sampling could add latency spikes; we will cap speculative attempts to 1 additional step and measure P95 impact.
Compatibility shim increases SDK complexity and duplicates some parse logic; plan to sunset shim after 3 months of adoption and document deprecation timeline.
Edge-case schemas (very large enums or regex validations) may be expensive; we will restrict runtime checks to structural validations and a small subset of high-value field checks.
False positives in schema scoring could preserve invalid beams; acceptance criteria focus on final payload validity rather than intermediate beam quality.
acceptance_criteria: Internal eval harness (see links) demonstrates >=99% JSON-schema pass rate on streaming tool-interleaved tests for the canary model (llama2-70b-instruct-quant) with feature on.
Median token-level latency increase <= 5% and P95 increase <= 10% on canary cluster under realistic load.
Compatibility shim successfully converts permissive interleaved frames into canonical JSON in >=98% of legacy SDK replay tests.
Automated regression tests added to CI covering: balanced brackets, missing-key recovery, enum enforcement, and tool-call marker tolerance.
Feature flag and control-plane toggles implemented; per-route metrics emitted (schema_compliance, speculative_recoveries, compatibility_rewrites).
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (3 days): prototype schema scoring function in Python eval harness; run on existing structured-output datasets and produce baseline metrics.
Phase 2 (5 days): implement prune hook and scoring in C++ serving runtime; add feature-flag gate; instrument metrics.
Phase 3 (4 days): build SDK compatibility shim that assembles permissive frames and documents migration steps for customers.
Phase 4 (2 days): create deterministic unit tests and chaos tests simulating partial tool outputs and truncated streams.
Phase 5 (ongoing): roll out to internal canaries → 5% hosted routes → ramp while monitoring.
test_plan: Synthetic interleaved tool-call corpus: 10k prompts with random tool-call insertions and partial JSON fragments; measure final schema pass rate.
Replay of customer anonymized failing traces from last 90 days (redacted) to ensure fixes address real failures.
Load test on canary cluster at 2x baseline QPS to capture latency tail behavior with feature enabled.
CI tests added: unit scoring tests, end-to-end streaming validator integration tests, and SDK shim roundtrip tests.
A/B experiment comparing current production decoder vs schema-aware beam prune on a subset of traffic for live validation.
rollout_plan: Enable internal-only routes for diagnostics and live debugging (day 0),
Canary: 1 model in internal canary fleet for 48–72 hours, monitor metrics and alerts (day 1–3),
Soft launch: expose feature flag to 5% of hosted routes with automatic rollback if schema_compliance_rate drops below 98% (day 4–10),
Gradual ramp to 50% and then full by triage of metrics and customer feedback (weeks 2–4).
docs_and_customer_communications: Add runtime flag docs to Console feature flags page with examples of expected behavior and migration steps for SDK users.
Post a migration guide in developer docs explaining the compatibility shim, expected deltas, and opt-out instructions.
Notify enterprise customers with Dedicated/Private deployments via account managers about planned rollout and opt-out windows.
